title: ME06a: The Napkin That Changed Everything
author: Richard Claydon
summary: Told as a short fable about a leader named Maya, this installment of Claydon's Leadership, Rewritten series argues that leaders develop best when development is built into the structure of the role rather than delivered through coaching or training. A mentor's napkin sketch of four quadrants, which Maya turns into Disciplined Delivery, Strategic Fluency, Adaptive Growth, and Relational Influence, becomes the basis for dual roles that pair a vertical market responsibility with a horizontal cross-boundary theme. She replaces task-list job descriptions with Self-in-Role-in-System briefs that name each leader's growth edge and the system pressures shaping them, illustrated through two leaders, Jo and Anil. The distinctive move is treating the brief as a mirror rather than a blueprint, so that the role itself becomes the developmental site. The piece closes with reflection prompts and sets up the next essay in the series, so it works as an opening of a longer sequence rather than a complete argument.
points: Maya's design premise is that leadership growth should come from structure, with dual vertical and horizontal roles that make people lead both with and without formal authority.
The four-quadrant map (Disciplined Delivery, Strategic Fluency, Adaptive Growth, Relational Influence) gives a lens for locating where a leader is under-stretched.
Self-in-Role-in-System briefs replace output-focused job descriptions by naming the personal growth edge and the organizational contradictions a role will press on.
The Jo and Anil examples show the same quadrant framework prescribing opposite moves, releasing control for one and holding tension for the other.
The closing reflection prompts turn the framework into a self-diagnostic any leader can apply to their own role.
quotes: They didn’t need superheroes. They needed co-developers of the system—people who could grow their own leadership, evolve their role, and influence across boundaries.
Traditional job descriptions list outputs. But they don’t show what a role does to a person.
Vertical roles carried executional authority. Horizontal roles carried evolutionary influence. Together, they stretched each leader across all four quadrants.
That was the difference. A blueprint told you what to build. A mirror told you who you were becoming while you built it.

By showing how the role was already entangling them with the system, the briefs turned everyday pressures into developmental sites. Instead of performing tasks for the system, each leader could begin to see how they might shape the system through the way they grew.

By naming stretch points explicitly, Maya did something unusual: she made leadership development part of the work itself. These weren’t add-on training programs. They were embedded invitations: grow here, in this role, under this pressure.
